initial_requirements: Marie Stopes International Uganda needs a Voucher Management Unit System for an output-based health program that subsidizes services through patient vouchers. Program staff should be able to create and distribute vouchers, record sales and treatment claims, validate claims from service providers, arrange eligible reimbursements, and monitor program results. The system should reduce manual processing while helping staff identify questionable or potentially fraudulent claims.

topics.topic_content: Internal program staff roles and responsibilities

slots.key: Program staff roles in voucher administration
slots.value: Program staff roles in voucher administration should generally be kept separate, especially validation and reimbursement approval, to maintain a clear check-and-balance. A person who creates or issues vouchers should not be the same person who approves reimbursement for claims tied to those vouchers. One person may perform more than one function only in a small office or when staffing is limited, but even then the system should record it clearly, and if possible require an extra approval or supervisor review. Such same-person handling should be allowed only in exceptional cases, such as very small teams or urgent operational needs with no alternative reviewer, and it must not happen silently; the system should require a reason, record an audit trail, and send the case for second-level supervisor approval before reimbursement is finalized. Rare exceptions may also be allowed during system downtime, emergency program response, or temporary staffing gaps during leave or travel, and any override should require a recorded justification and ideally approval from a supervisor or designated manager before use. Afterward, there should be mandatory review by finance or program management, with the audit log showing who overrode what and when. If possible, the override should be limited to a short time window or a single transaction. For adjustments, especially anything that changes claim amounts, it should not be handled by the same person who entered the original claim. If the same person entered the original claim, they should not be the one approving any payment-changing action, so the system needs a separate approver from the start.

slots.key: Approval authority for voucher issuance and claims
slots.value: Only authorized staff should be able to issue vouchers, validate claims, and approve reimbursements; every manual override, rejection, or approval must be recorded with a reason to maintain a traceable and defensible audit trail. Out-of-rule overrides should be very rare and may be allowed for emergency treatment, a system validation failure, a clearly documented exceptional approval from program management, or when a patient is eligible but one rule cannot be confirmed immediately and delaying care would cause harm. Only a designated senior supervisor or program manager should approve the override and record the reason and supporting notes; routine staff should not be able to grant that override on their own. Exceptional non-routine overrides are limited to emergency cases, verified system errors, or documented management decisions where waiting for the normal rule would block urgent service; for claims and reimbursements, they may also cover cases where the provider has completed the service but the paperwork is incomplete, provided management has reviewed and approved the case. The override must be available only to a senior role such as a program manager or designated supervisor, with a separate approval step and mandatory reason, notes, approver name, and timestamp, and the system should log the original rule that was bypassed for audit purposes. Override approval and cross-checking between validation and payment authorization are still tentative. If the same person both issues a voucher and validates or approves the related claim, that case must require a reason, audit trail recording, and second-level supervisor approval before reimbursement is finalized. Rare exceptions may also be allowed during system downtime, emergency program response, or temporary staffing gaps during leave or travel, and any override should require a recorded justification and ideally approval from a supervisor or designated manager before use. Afterward, there should be mandatory review by finance or program management, with the audit log showing who overrode what and when. If possible, the override should be limited to a short time window or a single transaction. Rejection should be allowed only for a claims officer or reviewer, but an override approval, reimbursement release, or any adjustment should need a supervisor or manager step as well. If the action changes money or payment status, there should be at least two levels of control in the first release, with the system logging who raised it and who approved it. If the normal approver is unavailable, it should route to an alternate supervisor or manager rather than letting the requester self-approve. For urgent cases, a fast-track exception is allowed only if the system still records the reason, the approving senior user, and any supporting note. If no authorised approver is available, the change should wait; urgency alone should not bypass control.

slots.value: Temporary changes to roles, settings, or claim rules must be recorded as a special administrative change, including the reason, who approved it, the start time, and when it was reversed. A genuine operational interruption can justify starting the change before approval is fully completed, but it must be tightly controlled and clearly marked as temporary; the system should keep the approval pending, show who initiated it, and force a follow-up sign-off and reversal note once the emergency is over. In takeover logging, the record should also capture who took over, who they were backing up for, the reason for the handover, what actions they performed, any records they touched, whether they made any temporary change to roles, settings, or claim handling, when the backup authority ended, who confirmed the handback if there was one, and any issues or exceptions that came up during the period.

slots.key: Timing between service delivery and claim submission

slots.key: Lost, voided, or replaced voucher handling
slots.value: If a voucher is lost, it should normally be marked inactive or cancelled once reported, so it can’t be redeemed again. If it’s voided because it was issued in error or the client was found ineligible, then it should be permanently invalid and not reused at all. A replacement voucher can only be issued if the original is confirmed unused or has been properly cancelled, and the system should keep the old one linked for audit purposes. If a voucher was already redeemed, then it should not be replaceable except through a formal correction process approved by a supervisor.

slots.key: Duplicate submission blocking and near-duplicate review
slots.value: Block clear same-duplicate submissions with no direct staff override; hold them until a supervisor or claims reviewer checks them. For near-duplicates, allow a review path where staff can add an explanation and supporting evidence. Overrides are only justified if the voucher was actually used for a different valid visit, or if the first entry was cancelled in error and there is proof from the provider or patient record; otherwise the submission should remain rejected or held.

topics.topic_content: Claim intake, validation, and exception handling

slots.value: In the first release, use only minimum checks to stop obviously bad data. At entry, the system should verify that the voucher number exists, is in the right format, and has not already been used or cancelled; that the sale or service date is a valid date, not in the future, and falls within the voucher’s active period; and that duplicate submissions with the same voucher number, patient, provider, and service date are blocked, with very close matches flagged for review. slots.key: Offline fallback and recovery for outages
slots.value: When the system is unavailable, staff should first switch to a manual fallback record such as a paper log or offline register so voucher, claim, or reimbursement details can be captured with timestamps, staff names, and any patient or provider reference available. Once the system is back, offline or paper records should be entered and reconciled so nothing is missed or duplicated.

slots.value: If the outage is short and the manual process is approved, staff can continue operating. slots.value: Only authorized staff should be able to issue vouchers, validate claims, and approve reimbursements; access should be limited based on role. Those roles should generally be kept separate, especially validation and reimbursement approval, to maintain a clear check-and-balance. A person who creates or issues vouchers should not be the same one who approves the reimbursement for claims tied to those vouchers. One person may perform more than one function only in a small office or when staffing is limited, and even then the system should record it clearly and, if possible, require an extra approval or supervisor review. In exceptional cases, the same person may issue a voucher and validate or approve the related claim only when the team is very small or there is an urgent operational need and no alternative reviewer is available; it must not be allowed silently, and it should require a reason, an audit trail, and second-level supervisor approval before reimbursement is finalized. In the first version, the sensitive steps should remain manual until staff are comfortable. Rejection should be allowed only for a claims officer or reviewer; override approval, reimbursement release, and any adjustment should require a supervisor or manager step as well. Fraud flags should be creatable by regular staff, but closing or clearing them should go to a more senior reviewer. If the action changes money or payment status, at least two levels of control are required in the first release, with logging of who raised it and who approved it. Adjustments that change claim amounts should not be handled by the same person who entered the original claim.

slots.key: Privacy and audit handling for sensitive information
slots.value: Sensitive client and provider information should be limited to staff who need it for their job, mainly voucher unit and authorized finance or operations staff. In most cases, others should only see the minimum necessary information, not the full sensitive details. Exceptions may be made for supervisors or auditors when reviewing a case, investigation, or compliance issue, but that access should be controlled and logged. Audit histories and record-change logs should be available to supervisors, compliance staff, and a small number of authorized administrators who need to investigate issues. Regular operational users probably should not have full access to all histories, especially if they only need to work on current records. Access should be more limited when the log contains sensitive client details or fraud-related notes, and separate permissions should be used for viewing versus editing corrective entries.

slots.key: Audit trail for manual decisions and overrides
slots.value: Every manual override, rejection, or approval should be recorded with a reason so the process remains traceable and defensible in case of audit. Any exception involving partial delivery, partial coverage, or excess beyond voucher coverage should also be recorded with a reason so the case is traceable. Exception cases such as supervisor-approved overrides for special vulnerability cases, data errors, or other program-approved exceptions should be tightly controlled, clearly flagged in the system, and the reason recorded with approval traceable. For manual review outcomes, the reviewer’s decision must be recorded and visible in the audit trail. Overrides should be very rare and may be used for emergency treatment, a system validation failure, a clearly documented exceptional approval from program management, or when a patient is eligible but one rule cannot be confirmed immediately and delaying care would cause harm. Only a designated senior supervisor or program manager may approve the override, and the approver must record the reason and supporting notes; routine staff cannot grant the override on their own. It should be limited to exceptional cases like an emergency, a verified system error, or a documented management decision where waiting for the normal rule would block urgent service. For claims and reimbursements, it could also cover cases where the provider has done the service and the paperwork is incomplete, but the case has been reviewed and approved by management. The system should make those overrides available only to a senior role like a program manager or designated supervisor, with a separate approval step and mandatory reason, notes, and the approver’s name and timestamp. It should also log the original rule that was bypassed so we can audit why the override happened. The log should include any issues or exceptions that came up during the backup period. If the same person issues a voucher and validates or approves the related claim, the system should require a reason, record an audit trail, and route the case for second-level supervisor approval before reimbursement is finalized. In rare exceptions like system downtime, emergency program response, or temporary staffing gaps during leave or travel, the override needs recorded justification, ideally prior approval from a supervisor or designated manager, mandatory after-the-fact review by finance or program management, an audit log showing who overrode what and when, and a short time window or single-transaction limit if possible. In the first version, sensitive steps like claim rejection, override approval, fraud flags, and reimbursement release should stay manual until staff are comfortable. For clear same-duplicates, staff should not be able to override them directly; they must stay blocked until a supervisor or claims reviewer checks them. For near-duplicates, staff may use a review path where they add an explanation and supporting evidence. An override is only justified if they can show the voucher was actually used for a different valid visit, or the first entry was cancelled in error with proof from the provider or patient record. Without solid evidence, the submission should remain rejected or held rather than forced through.

slots.key: Support role continuity and backup coverage
slots.value: Support should not be tied to only one administrator; at least two approved people should be able to take over critical support tasks, with access controls that do not require sharing personal passwords. If the usual administrator is unavailable, an authorized backup person should be able to handle urgent issues and keep operations moving. The log should capture who took over and who they were backing up for.

slots.value: Key documentation should be kept current, including user roles, configuration settings, claim rules, and reporting procedures. For continuity when the usual administrator or support owner is unavailable, the backup person should rely on current user and workflow documentation, plus the active claim queue, pending approvals, and exception logs, and should be able to update a handover note or incident log showing what they took over, when, and from whom. If the handover is incomplete, outdated, or doesn’t match the current live situation, the backup person should not just proceed on their own; they need a quick sign-off from the senior owner or at least a confirmation in the incident log before taking over anything sensitive. The log should also record the reason for the handover and the time it started.

topics.topic_content: Questionable and potentially fraudulent claim detection

slots.value: Questionable or potentially fraudulent claims; system should monitor performance and possible fraud and quickly spot anything that looks suspicious, including invalid vouchers, duplicate use, missing information, suspicious claim patterns, repeated claims, unusual patterns, and mismatched provider and patient details. It should also flag claims with late submissions, repeated corrections, a history of previously rejected claims, already used vouchers, the same patient or voucher number appearing too often, unusually many exceptions from a provider, very high claim volume in a short period, services that do not fit the normal pattern for that facility, or claims that are technically complete but still inconsistent with past history.

revisions.new_value: If a claim is flagged as questionable, it must go to a separate review path and not pass straight through normal validation or reimbursement. It should be reviewed by a designated senior claims reviewer or fraud-control staff, ideally not the same person who first handled it. The claim should be held until extra evidence is attached and the reviewer clears it, or escalated to management if the issue is serious. If still unresolved, it stays on hold and the reason must be shown clearly so nobody accidentally pays it.

slots.value: Claims matching a known bad actor, a previously used voucher, or a suspicious duplicate should be blocked or sent straight to review; watchlist and blacklist logic should especially apply to providers and vouchers, and possibly clients if repeated abuse patterns are found. In practice, providers can submit claims and receive status updates, but if they are blacklisted or under review the system should stop payment and clearly show the claim as under hold or rejected. For clients, a watchlist or blacklist match should let staff pause voucher use or distribution until the issue is cleared. External organizations or sites that are restricted should not be processed normally until an authorized user lifts the restriction, and any later re-enablement must include a proper approval trail showing who decided and why. Anything new from a restricted organization, partner, or site should be blocked from submission while the restriction is active; items already in progress should be put on hold rather than deleted, preserving the record until an authorized person reviews it. Whether held items are later resumed or rejected depends on the reason for the restriction and the length of the hold.

slots.value: Those roles should generally be kept separate, especially validation and reimbursement approval, because a clear check-and-balance is needed. A person who creates or issues vouchers should not be the same one who approves the reimbursement for claims tied to those vouchers. In exceptional cases only, such as a very small team or an urgent operational need with no alternative reviewer available, the same person may both issue a voucher and validate or approve the related claim, but not silently. The system should require a reason, record an audit trail, and route the case for second-level supervisor approval before reimbursement is finalized so accountability is preserved and potential conflicts of interest can be reviewed later. If the same person entered the original claim, they should not approve any payment-changing action; the system must use a separate approver from the start. If the normal approver is unavailable, the request should route to an alternate supervisor or manager rather than allowing requester self-approval. For urgent cases, a fast-track exception is allowed only if the system records the reason, the approving senior user, and any supporting note; urgency alone must not bypass control, and if no authorised approver is available the change must wait.

slots.key: Operational controls to reduce manual work and detect suspicious claims

slots.key: Audit logging, role management, and outage recovery support
slots.value: Audit histories and record-change logs should be available to supervisors, compliance staff, and a small number of authorized administrators who need to investigate issues. Regular operational users should not have full access to all histories if they only need to work on current records. Access should be more limited when logs contain sensitive client details or fraud-related notes, and separate permissions may be needed for viewing versus editing corrective entries. The original entry should stay visible, corrections should only be made by authorized users such as supervisors or back-office admins, and the system should record what was changed, who changed it, when, and why. If the error affects payment or reimbursement, the correction should retain the link to the original transaction so the full history remains visible. The support role should not be tied to only one administrator; at least two approved people should be able to take over critical support tasks without sharing personal passwords. Key documentation should stay current, especially user roles, configuration settings, claim rules, and reporting procedures. If the usual administrator is unavailable, an authorized backup person should be able to manage urgent issues and keep operations moving. Every exchange should have a reference and a timestamp, and each status change should be logged, especially for submission, validation, approval, rejection, and reimbursement. If there is supporting evidence for a fraud flag, the system should allow attaching documents or references to the related claim records so later reviewers can see exactly what was observed. That traceability is important because the flag must be justifiable even if fraud is not yet proven.

slots.value: Alternative evidence should only be accepted when it clearly ties the voucher, patient, service date, and provider together, even if the original document is missing. Acceptable examples include a signed treatment record, stock register entry, discharge note, or verified field follow-up, as long as it matches the claim details and is authenticated. Hold or manual escalation is required if dates do not match, the patient cannot be traced, provider details look wrong, the same evidence is being reused, or the amounts claimed do not fit the service provided. If there is any sign of tampering, duplicate claiming, or missing core proof for a high-risk case, it should not be auto-approved.

topics.topic_content: Data retention, audit history, and record traceability

slots.value: The audit trail should show who did the action, when it happened, what record was affected, and the before-and-after values where possible. Core identifiers should always be present, even if a voucher is reversed or corrected, so the original record can still be traced. Later-step fields can be blank if the transaction never reached that stage, but the system should clearly show that they were not applicable rather than hiding them. Status and reason should remain visible so the audit trail stays complete. If the same person both issues a voucher and validates or approves the related claim, the system must require a reason, record an audit trail, and preserve accountability so conflict of interest can be checked later. For overrides, the log should also show who overrode what and when, plus the reason for the override, the approving person, the specific transaction or voucher affected, whether it was a one-time exception or had an expiry time, any usage limit set, the user who performed the action, the old and new status before and after the override, and any comments attached by the reviewer. If the action changes money or payment status, the system should log who raised it and who approved it.

slots.value: The first version should include backup or outage handling so records can be managed during downtime and restored afterward. During downtime, staff should switch to a manual fallback record such as a paper log or offline register to capture voucher, claim, or reimbursement details with timestamps, staff names, and any patient or provider reference available; once the system is back, transactions can be entered and reconciled against the manual record. If the downtime is short and the manual process is approved, they can continue; if the outage affects validation, duplicate checking, or payment approval in a way that could create errors, they should stop and wait for the system or an authorized override rather than continue operating.

slots.value: The system should include enough documentation or handover notes for another person to pick up maintenance work if staff change over time, and key documentation should stay current, especially user roles, configuration settings, claim rules, and reporting procedures. The backup person should be able to rely on current user and workflow documentation, plus any active claim queue, pending approvals, and exception logs, and should be able to update a handover note or incident log showing what they took over, when, and from whom. If the handover is incomplete, outdated, or does not match the current live situation, the backup person should not proceed on their own; they need a quick sign-off from the senior owner or at least confirmation in the incident log before taking over anything sensitive.

slots.value: Temporary changes to roles, settings, or claim rules should be recorded as a special administrative change, including the reason, who approved it, the start time, and when it was reversed. It should only be allowed when there is a genuine operational interruption, such as the main administrator being unreachable, a deadline is at risk, or claim processing would stop entirely without the change. Normally it should need approval from a senior manager or designated system owner, and the reason should be logged before it takes effect. In a true emergency, the change may start first and be regularized immediately after, but it must be tightly controlled and clearly marked as temporary. The system should keep the approval pending, show who initiated it, and force a follow-up sign-off and reversal note once the emergency is over. If staff are changing roles, settings, or claim rules rather than just following documented steps, that should require extra logging and probably prior approval if time allows. Overrides should be limited to rare exceptions like system downtime, emergency program response, or temporary staffing gaps, and should be time-boxed or restricted to a single transaction when possible.

slots.value: If a backup person proceeds during urgent operational continuity, the system should clearly record that they acted as backup and why, plus who took over, who they were backing up for, the reason for the handover, when it started, what actions they performed, any records they touched, whether they made temporary changes to roles, settings, or claim handling, when the backup authority ended, who confirmed the handback if there was one, and any issues or exceptions that came up during the period. It should also capture the exact state they stepped into, especially whether the work was at intake, validation, exception review, reimbursement prep, or already flagged for fraud review, plus any open task, the claim or voucher reference, and whether the item was partially processed or waiting on someone else.

slots.value: A person may override the normal separation of duties only in rare exceptions such as system downtime, emergency program response, or temporary staffing gaps during leave or travel. The override should require a recorded justification and ideally approval from a supervisor or designated manager before use. Afterward, finance or program management must review it. The audit record for the override should be kept for the full program retention period, expected to be several years after the claim or voucher is closed, should never be deleted, should not be edited except by a new logged entry correcting it, and should be viewable only by a very small number of administrators, with later review available to finance, program management, and internal audit. For the first release, actions that change money or payment status should have at least two levels of control.

slots.value: The claim is validated against voucher details, eligibility rules, and any service limits before reimbursement is approved; claims must match the supported service under the program and should be held or rejected if missing, inconsistent, duplicate, outside allowed dates, above the permitted limit, suspicious, or mismatched in provider/patient details. If a service is only partially delivered or only partly covered, the claim should be adjusted to the payable portion or held for review if the split is not clear. If the service exceeds what the voucher covers, the excess amount should be identified separately so staff can decide whether to reject it or bill it outside the program, depending on the rules. Exceptions must be recorded with a reason for traceability. Validation should also check that the service date falls within the voucher validity period, the provider is active and participating, the claim has not already been redeemed or submitted before, and all required fields and supporting documents are complete; at entry, the system should verify that the voucher number exists, is in the right format, and has not already been used or cancelled, that the sale or service date is a valid date, not in the future, and within the voucher’s active period, and that duplicate submissions for the same voucher number, patient, provider, and service date are blocked while near-duplicates are flagged for review. Clearly bad entries such as missing patient identity, negative or zero claim amounts, and unregistered providers should be blocked at entry. The system should also block claims unless the voucher is tied to a valid patient and a registered provider, the service type is a supported service, the claim amount is present, numeric, and within the expected range for that service, required dates are in the right order such as service date before claim submission date, and mandatory fields are not blank.

slots.value: Budget limits and reimbursement caps will apply to control program spend, but the exact amounts and whether they apply per voucher, per claim, per provider, or per period are still to be confirmed with finance and program management. The system should support configurable limits rather than hardcoded ones so they can be adjusted if program rules change.

slots.value: Only a designated senior supervisor or program manager may approve a rare out-of-rule override; routine staff must not be able to grant the override on their own. Overrides are limited to exceptional cases such as an emergency, a verified system error, or a documented management decision where waiting for the normal rule would block urgent service. For claims and reimbursements, an override can also apply when the provider has already delivered the service but the paperwork is incomplete, provided management has reviewed and approved the case. For same-duplicate submissions, staff must not be able to override directly; the item should stay blocked until a supervisor or claims reviewer checks it. Near-duplicates may follow a review path where staff can add an explanation and supporting evidence. If the requester entered the original claim, they must not approve the payment-changing action; the system should route to a separate approver from the start. If the normal approver is unavailable, the action should route to an alternate supervisor or manager rather than allowing self-approval. Urgent cases may use a fast-track exception only when the system still records the reason, the approving senior user, and any supporting note; urgency alone must not bypass control. If no authorised approver is available, the change should wait.

slots.key: Manual review handling by issue severity
slots.value: Claims with warning signs should be handled according to severity: low-risk warnings can proceed if the core documents are complete, while medium and high-risk warnings require supporting evidence before approval. If evidence is still weak or inconsistent, the claim should stay on hold until stronger proof is provided or the case is escalated for manual review. Alternative evidence may be acceptable when one document is missing, such as strong proof from the service provider, patient record, or field verification.

revisions.new_value: Claims should be handled differently depending on the type of concern: serious issues such as likely duplicates, invalid vouchers, or clear eligibility mismatches should be held before payment until reviewed; minor inconsistencies can be paid but flagged for monitoring, provided the reviewer’s decision is recorded and visible in the audit trail.

If unresolved, it must remain on hold with the reason clearly shown so it cannot be paid accidentally.

slots.key: Routine administrator audit trail visibility and retention maintenance
slots.value: Routine administrators may review the full audit trail, including who did the action, when it happened, what record was affected, and before-and-after values where possible. They may maintain standard retention settings for documents and transactions only if those settings are already approved by the program; changing retention settings should be restricted to a smaller set of approved users, not everyone in administration. Routine administrators should be able to view audit history across the records they are responsible for, but some sensitive record types, such as payment-related or flagged fraud cases, may need to be view-only for some staff even if they can manage ordinary records. Only a very small number of administrators should be able to view the override audit record, and they should not be able to edit it.

slots.key: Backup administrator documentation and handover logging
slots.value: Backup personnel should update a handover note or incident log showing who took over, who they were backing up for, the reason for the handover, when it started, what actions they performed, any records they touched, and whether they made any temporary change to roles, settings, or claim handling. The log should also show when the backup authority ended, who confirmed the handback if there was one, any issues or exceptions that came up during the period, and the exact state they stepped into (especially whether work was at intake, validation, exception review, reimbursement prep, or already flagged for fraud review), plus any open task, claim or voucher reference, and whether the item was partially processed or waiting on someone else.

slots.key: Role separation for voucher issuance, claim validation, and reimbursement approval
slots.value: Claim rejection should be allowed only for a claims officer or reviewer. Override approval, reimbursement release, and any adjustment should require a supervisor or manager step as well. Fraud flags may be created by regular staff, but closing or clearing them should be handled by a more senior reviewer. If an action changes money or payment status, the first release should have at least two levels of control, with the system logging who raised it and who approved it. Adjustments that change claim amounts should not be handled by the same person who entered the original claim.

revisions.new_value: Voucher issuance/creation should be kept separate from claim validation and reimbursement approval, with validation and reimbursement approval especially separated to preserve check-and-balance controls. A person who creates or issues vouchers should not be the same person who approves reimbursement for claims tied to those vouchers. One person may perform more than one of these functions only in a small office or when staffing is limited, and even then the system should clearly record it and, if possible, require an extra approval or supervisor review.

sections.section_content: Operational Quality, Security, Privacy, and System Resilience

topics.topic_content: User access control and data protection

slots.value: Only staff who need sensitive client and provider information for their job should access it, mainly voucher unit and authorized finance or operations staff. Others should generally see only the minimum necessary information, not full sensitive details. Supervisors or auditors may access it when reviewing a case, investigation, or compliance issue, but that access must be controlled and logged. Strong user roles are needed. Any exception access outside normal rules should be tightly controlled, clearly flagged in the system, and require recorded reasons plus traceable approval. The support role should not be tied to only one administrator, and access controls should allow at least two approved people to take over critical support tasks without sharing personal passwords. Routine administrators should be able to manage users, reset passwords, assign roles, update voucher batches, run standard reports, and make simple configuration changes like adjusting reference data or basic workflow settings within approved limits. Anything affecting core business rules, payment logic, fraud detection rules, or system integrations should require specialist approval or developer support.

slots.value: Client and provider information should be limited to staff who need it for their job, with only minimum necessary information shown to others. Exceptions may be made for supervisors or auditors during case reviews, investigations, or compliance checks, and such access must be controlled and logged. Any access allowed outside the normal rules should be tightly controlled, clearly flagged, and include a recorded reason with traceable approval. An override should be very rare, limited to situations such as emergency treatment, a system validation failure, a clearly documented exceptional approval from program management, or when a patient is eligible but one rule cannot be confirmed immediately and delaying care would cause harm. Only a designated senior supervisor or program manager may approve the override, and the approver must record the reason and supporting notes. Routine staff cannot grant the override on their own. In rare exceptions such as system downtime, emergency program response, or temporary staffing gaps during leave or travel, the override should require a recorded justification and ideally approval from a supervisor or designated manager before use, followed by mandatory review by finance or program management, with the audit log showing who overrode what and when. If possible, the override should be limited to a short time window or a single transaction.

slots.value: The system should record what was changed, who changed it, when, and why, and every status change should be logged with a reference and a timestamp. This supports traceability across submission, validation, approval, rejection, and reimbursement. The status and reason should remain visible even if a voucher is canceled, reversed, or adjusted, so the audit trail remains complete. When someone acts as backup, the system should clearly record that they acted as backup and why. The log should also capture who took over, who they were backing up for, the reason for the handover, the time it started, what actions they performed, any records they touched, whether they made any temporary change to roles, settings, or claim handling, when the backup authority ended, who confirmed the handback if there was one, any issues or exceptions that came up during the period, and the exact claim state they stepped into, including whether the work was at intake, validation, exception review, reimbursement prep, or flagged for fraud review, plus any open task, claim or voucher reference, and whether the item was already partially processed or waiting on someone else. For overrides, the log should capture the reason for the override, the approving person, the specific transaction or voucher affected, whether it was a one-time exception or had an expiry time, any usage limit set, the user who performed the action, the old and new status before and after the override, and any comments attached by the reviewer. The audit record should be kept for the full program retention period, expected to be several years after the claim or voucher is closed, should never be deleted, should not be edited, and if correction is needed it should be done through a new logged entry rather than changing the original record. When a fraud flag is created, it should also capture who raised the flag, the time, the voucher or claim reference, the specific reason category, a free-text note explaining what looked wrong in plain language, and any supporting evidence through attached documents or references to the related claim records so later reviewers can see exactly what was observed.

slots.key: Role separation for vouchers, claims validation, and reimbursement approval
slots.value: Those roles should generally be kept separate, especially validation and reimbursement approval, to maintain a clear check-and-balance. A person who creates or issues vouchers should not be the same one who approves reimbursement for claims tied to those vouchers. One person may do more than one function only in a small office or when staffing is limited, but in those cases the system should record it clearly and, if possible, require extra approval or supervisor review. It should only happen in exceptional cases, such as when the team is very small or there is an urgent operational need and no alternative reviewer is available. If the same person does both, the system should require a reason, record an audit trail, and route the case for a second-level supervisor approval before reimbursement is finalized.

revisions.new_value: Routine field or operations staff can issue vouchers, claims staff can validate claims, and finance or senior management should approve reimbursements. The exact role names and whether one person can hold more than one of these permissions still need confirmation. Override approval and any cross-checking between validation and payment authorization are still tentative.

slots.key: Fraud-flagged claim review routing and hold conditions
slots.value: Claims should use warning sign severity as a guide, but the final decision must follow a review rule set agreed by the program team and finance. Low-risk warnings can proceed if the core documents are complete. Medium and high-risk warnings require supporting evidence before approval. Alternative evidence can be accepted when one document is missing if there is other strong proof from the service provider, patient record, or field verification. If evidence is still weak or inconsistent, the claim should stay on hold until stronger proof is provided or the case is escalated for manual review.

revisions.new_value: Claims flagged as questionable should bypass normal validation and reimbursement and go through a separate review path. They should be reviewed by a designated senior claims reviewer or fraud-control staff, preferably not the same person who first handled the claim. The claim should remain on hold until extra evidence is attached and the reviewer clears it. If the issue is serious, it should be escalated to management. If unresolved, it must stay on hold and clearly display the reason so it is not accidentally paid.

revisions.old_value: Claims flagged as questionable should bypass normal validation and reimbursement and go through a separate review path. If unresolved, it must stay on hold and clearly display the reason so it is not accidentally paid.
revisions.new_value: Claims with clear warning signs should go straight to a separate review queue right away, including obvious mismatches, duplicate-looking claims, or anything tied to a known exception pattern. Only mild concerns can stay in the normal queue until a reviewer confirms special handling. Once separated, the system should make that status very visible.

revisions.new_value: Claims with warning signs should have the evidence requirement vary by warning sign. For a simple mismatch, acceptable supporting evidence may include a corrected document, a verified service note, or a provider explanation. For duplicate or suspicious claims, stronger proof is needed, such as original registers, patient confirmation, or cross-checks against treatment records. The system should not let the claim leave review until the evidence is attached and the reviewer has marked it as acceptable; if evidence is incomplete, the claim should remain on hold and the reason should be easy to see.

These cases should go to review even when the amount itself looks normal.

slots.key: First-version task simplification and manual controls
slots.value: In the first version, common tasks should be very simple, including creating a voucher, searching a patient or claim, recording a sale, and submitting a claim in a few clear screens. Shortcuts such as default values, dropdowns, and prefilled provider or patient details should be used to help staff learn quickly. More sensitive steps should remain manual at first, including claim rejection, override approval, fraud flags, reimbursement release, and any adjustments or exceptions, so staff must confirm them carefully until they are comfortable.

slots.key: Approval levels for money-changing or payment-status actions
slots.value: Any action that changes money or payment status should require at least two levels of control in the first release, with the system logging who raised it and who approved it. The requester must not self-approve if they entered the original claim; a separate approver should be assigned from the start. If the normal approver is unavailable, the request should route to an alternate supervisor or manager. For duplicates, it should block the same voucher number, patient, provider, and service date combination if it has already been submitted, and flag anything very close to that for review. Clearly bad cases to block include missing patient identity, negative or zero claim amounts, and a provider that is not registered in the system. Claims failing these basics should be blocked from going forward for review until corrected.

topics.topic_content: Validation criteria and unresolved decision points

slots.key: Acceptance criteria for voucher issuance and claim approval
slots.value: Approve only if the patient or service is eligible, the voucher is valid, and the claim details match the supported service under the program. Missing, inconsistent, duplicate, outside allowed dates, or above-permitted-limit cases should not pass straight through; they should be held for review or rejected depending on severity. Suspicious cases such as repeated claims, unusual patterns, or mismatched provider and patient details should be flagged for manual review, but the current set of manual review triggers is tentative for now and should remain adjustable later without major rework. Finalizing any additional triggers should be confirmed with the program and finance teams before locking in the fraud rules. For questionable claims, the system should require supporting evidence before the claim leaves review, and the evidence must be attached and marked acceptable by the reviewer; if evidence is incomplete, the claim stays on hold and the reason should be visible. The system should prefill checks when the same verification pattern repeats often, such as matching voucher numbers, provider details, dates, and service type against the claim. It should also suggest the usual supporting documents based on the claim category so staff do not have to remember every step each time. Claims should be flagged for review beyond the basic warning signs if the amounts are unusual, the same provider has many exceptions, or the claim conflicts with prior voucher or treatment history, even if they were not manually marked as questionable. The specific checks and supporting documents shown should depend on the claim type, service category, provider, and any risk indicators already attached to the claim. Routine claims should show the standard verification items, while exceptions or prior issues should also prompt extra checks relevant to that case. In some cases, the system should deliberately leave items blank for the reviewer to decide where the evidence depends on judgment or the situation is not clear from the record. A voucher should stop being treated as a near-duplicate when there is a clear business reason that distinguishes it from the earlier submission, especially when the patient, provider, and service date are different in a meaningful way or the service is a different approved service. Small spelling or formatting differences, or a slight amount change / single-field correction while everything else stays the same, should still trigger a duplicate warning unless the underlying service is truly different and can be supported. For first-release minimum data checks, the system should also verify that the voucher is tied to a valid patient and a registered provider, that the service type is supported, that the claim amount is present, numeric, and within the expected range for that service, that required dates are in the correct order such as service date before claim submission date, and that mandatory fields are not blank. Claims failing those basics should be blocked from review until corrected.

slots.key: Restriction handling for in-progress vouchers, redemptions, and claims
slots.value: New submissions from a restricted organization, partner, or site should be blocked while the restriction is active. Items already in progress should be put on hold rather than deleted so the record is preserved, and after review they may be resumed or rejected depending on the reason for the restriction and the length of the hold. If a voucher is lost, it should normally be marked inactive or cancelled once reported, so it can’t be redeemed again. If it’s voided because it was issued in error or the client was found ineligible, it should be permanently invalid and not reused at all. A replacement voucher can only be issued if the original is confirmed unused or has been properly cancelled, and the system should keep the old one linked for audit purposes. If a voucher was already redeemed, then it should not be replaceable except through a formal correction process approved by a supervisor. Core identifiers should always remain present, even if a voucher is reversed or corrected, so the original record stays traceable. Later-step fields may be blank if the transaction never reached that stage, but the system should clearly show those fields as not applicable rather than hiding them. Status and reason should stay visible so the audit trail remains complete.

slots.key: Exception cases for out-of-rule coverage approval
slots.value: Exception cases should be very rare and may include emergency treatment, a verified system error, a clearly documented exceptional approval from program management, or cases where a patient appears eligible but one rule cannot be confirmed immediately and delaying care would cause harm. For claims and reimbursements, the override can also apply when the provider has already performed the service but the paperwork is incomplete, provided the case has been reviewed and approved by management. Only a designated senior supervisor or program manager may approve the override, with a separate approval step and mandatory reason, supporting notes, approver name, and timestamp. The system must also log the original rule that was bypassed for audit purposes. If it is a clear same-duplicate, staff should not be able to override it directly; it should stay blocked until a supervisor or claims reviewer checks it. For near-duplicates, staff may add an explanation and supporting evidence for review. An override is only justified if the voucher was actually used for a different valid visit, or if the first entry was cancelled in error and there is proof from the provider or patient record. If there is no solid evidence, it should remain rejected or held rather than forced through. Rejection should be allowed only for a claims officer or reviewer, while override approval, reimbursement release, and any adjustment require a supervisor or manager step as well. Fraud flags may be created by regular staff, but closing or clearing them should go to a more senior reviewer. Any action that changes money or payment status should require at least two levels of control on first release, with the system logging who raised it and who approved it. Adjustments that change claim amounts should not be handled by the same person who entered the original claim.

slots.key: Evidence requirements by warning sign severity
slots.value: The system should use warning sign severity as a guide, but the final decision must be based on a review rule set agreed by the program team and finance. Low-risk warnings can proceed if the core documents are complete. Medium and high-risk warnings require supporting evidence before approval. Alternative evidence is acceptable only when it clearly ties the voucher, patient, service date, and provider together, even if the original document is missing. Acceptable examples include a signed treatment record, stock register entry, discharge note, or verified field follow-up, provided they match the claim details and are authenticated. If dates do not match, the patient cannot be traced, provider details look wrong, the same evidence is reused, or the amounts claimed do not fit the service provided, the case should be held or manually escalated. Any sign of tampering, duplicate claiming, or missing core proof in a high-risk case should prevent auto-approval.

revisions.new_value: Evidence requirements vary by warning sign: for a simple mismatch, acceptable evidence may include a corrected document, a verified service note, or a provider explanation; for duplicate or suspicious claims, stronger proof is expected, such as original registers, patient confirmation, or cross-checks against treatment records.
